13: # Core Rules
14: 
15: ## Language & Communication
16: - Chat with the user in Russian.
17: - Keep code comments, docstrings, user-facing string literals, and git commit messages in English.
18: 
19: ## Engineering Workflow
20: - Verify information before stating it.
21: - Preserve existing behavior unless the user explicitly requests a change.
22: - Make minimal, focused edits and avoid unrelated cleanup.
23: - Do not propose whitespace-only changes.
24: - Do not invent changes beyond the user's request.
25: - Prefer single coherent patches per file.
26: 
27: ## Completion Discipline
28: - Do not mark work complete without verifying the result in a task-appropriate way.
29: - If verification is partial or unavailable, state that explicitly and name the remaining risk.
30: - For bug fixes, prefer confirming the root cause or the most likely failure path before closing the task.
31: 
32: ## General Engineering Principles
33: - Prefer small, coherent changes.
34: - Keep functions small and single-purpose.
35: - Use meaningful names and avoid unclear abbreviations.
36: - Replace magic values with named constants or configuration.
37: - Keep file and module structure coherent and predictable.
38: - Hide implementation details behind clear interfaces and module boundaries.
39: - Use comments only to explain intent or non-obvious decisions.
40: - Refactor early when debt becomes visible.
41: - Add or update focused tests for bug fixes, edge cases, and error paths when the project has testing in place.
42: 
43: ## DRY
44: - Do not duplicate code.
45: - If duplication is detected or strongly suspected, tell the user and propose a refactoring path.
46: ## Git Workflow
47: - Never create commits on `main`, `master`, `develop`, or `staging` by default.
48: - If currently on one of those branches, warn the user and suggest creating a new branch.
49: - Direct commits on protected branches are allowed only when the user explicitly authorizes them for the current task, and only for small follow-up changes tightly coupled to work that has just been merged or released.
50: - Do not use the protected-branch exception for new feature work, broad refactors, or behavior changes that should receive their own branch lifecycle.
51: - Always ask the user to approve the commit message text before committing.
52: - Exception: during a run of the `autonomous-task-run` skill, the instruction to run autonomously is the standing approval of the commit flow — commit messages follow the project's standard form without per-commit approval. Pushing still requires explicit approval.
53: - Extract the SCM task id from branch names shaped as `<purpose>/<task_id>-<description>`.
54: - Use commit messages in the form `task_id. (commit_type) commit_message.`
55: ## Error Handling
56: - Functions must either return a valid result or raise an exception with actionable context.
57: - Never swallow exceptions.
58: - Never return `None`, empty collections, or magic values to hide an error.
59: - Use exception chaining when translating low-level failures.
60: - Use `Optional[T]` only for legitimate absence of a value, not for error signaling.
61: ## Retrieval Routing
62: 
63: Stored knowledge is not conversation context. Retrieve it when relevant; do not preload it merely because it exists. Keep accumulated project knowledge outside the active context by default and retrieve only the smallest relevant subset the current task needs.
64: 
65: - Before broad repository exploration, determine what information is missing and query the narrowest available knowledge source capable of answering it.
66: - When an enabled retrieval capability directly matches the current information need, use it before falling back to broader manual exploration.
67: - Route retrieval according to the kind of information required, not according to tool familiarity.
68: - Retrieval narrows the evidence set; it does not establish correctness or completeness by itself.
69: - Verify retrieved claims against their authoritative source before relying on them for implementation or review when correctness matters.
70: - Prefer narrow retrieval before broad retrieval, and broad retrieval before indiscriminate repository scanning.
71: - At the start of non-trivial discovery, identify which enabled retrieval capabilities match the task before choosing an exploration strategy; do not invoke every capability ceremonially — use one when it can materially narrow the search.
72: 
73: ### Routing Table
74: 
75: | Information need | Preferred source |
76: |---|---|
77: | previous task state, prior local decisions, discovered project patterns, unresolved investigations | project memory (local working memory) |
78: | canonical project decisions, architecture, and domain rules | Git-tracked documentation under `docs/domain/**`, `docs/decisions/**`, `docs/architecture/**` |
79: | semantic code discovery, analogous implementations, unknown implementation location | semantic code search (Chroma) |
80: | exact symbol or file already known | direct source access |
81: | call or dependency paths, impact analysis across modules | structural code intelligence (when enabled) |
82: | final verification | canonical docs, source code, and tests |
83: 
84: ### Capability And Implementation
85: 
86: - Capabilities are named independently of the tools implementing them: project memory may be backed by Basic Memory, semantic code search by Chroma, structural code intelligence by a graph tool.
87: - Swapping an implementation backend must not require rewriting these behavioral rules.
88: ## Project Memory
89: 
90: Local cross-session working memory keeps what the agent learned and where the work stands — outside Git history and outside canonical documentation.
91: 
92: - Keep local working memory under `docs/local/**`, gitignored by default (add `/docs/local/` to `.gitignore`); a project may relocate the tree via `[project_memory]` in the manifest.
93: - Never treat local working memory as canonical project documentation.
94: - Do not write temporary task state, speculative findings, or session continuation data into canonical documentation merely to preserve agent context.
95: - Promotion from local working memory to canonical documentation is an explicit semantic operation, never an automatic synchronization step: promote only knowledge that has become durable, and only when the user or the project workflow permits the corresponding canonical artifact.
96: - Memory is a curated state store, not an execution log: record what future sessions need, not what merely happened.
97: 
98: ### Taxonomy
99: 
100: - `context/` — goal, scope, constraints, accepted direction, current phase, relevant artifacts, immediate next step. Not a transcript.
101: - `decisions/` — what has been decided locally and why: decision, reason, scope, and status (`provisional`, `confirmed`, `superseded`, `rejected`). Record a local decision when it materially constrains subsequent work; a local `confirmed` decision is confirmed for the current work context and does not automatically become a canonical record.
102: - `progress/` — where the work stopped: `done`, `current`, `blocked`, `next`. Update at meaningful phase boundaries and before ending work expected to continue in another session.
103: - `patterns/` — reusable project properties discovered during work. Treat a discovered pattern as working knowledge until validated against source code or canonical documentation; update or supersede it when contrary evidence appears; do not accumulate contradictory memories without recording their relationship.
104: - `investigations/` — open questions and the evidence found so far, with lifecycle `open`, `resolved`, or `abandoned`. An investigation may disappear, produce a pattern or a decision, or require human consultation.
105: - `handoffs/` — resume points: goal, confirmed state, current state, open questions, next action, links to relevant memory. Sufficient to resume without replaying the conversation, compact enough to inspect before loading more context.
106: 
107: The semantic categories are the standard; the physical split into directories may be configured per project.
108: 
109: ### Write And Read Policy
110: 
111: Write to local memory when the information will be needed in a later session, materially affects further decisions, is expensive to reconstruct, is the result of an investigation, explains the current status, captures an unresolved question or blocker, or is a confirmed reusable project pattern. Do not write what a single obvious file already says, transient tool output, reasoning detail, what already exists canonically, a guess with no useful role, or a duplicate that changes no state.
112: 
113: Query local memory by the current goal, relevant entities, modules, concepts, decisions, and task identifiers — never read the whole memory tree at session start. To continue previous work: retrieve the relevant context, then the current progress, then the relevant decisions; open patterns and investigations only as the current step requires.
114: 
115: ### Note Shape And Durable Lessons
116: 
117: - Minimal frontmatter: `title`, `type`, `status`, `updated`, plus `source` when the note records a discovered fact. Canonical-note body requirements — `## Observations` and `## Relations` sections — do not apply inside the local memory area, and local notes never mix into canonical zones.
118: - Name every Markdown document created in the local memory area `YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>.md`, exactly the notation of canonical dated artifacts. The date is the note's creation date: content updates never rename the note, and a hygiene merge keeps the older date. The payoff is direct: a note promoted into canonical documentation keeps its file name, and name collisions across the two areas stay rare.
119: - After meaningful corrections or repeated mistakes, capture only durable lessons that can prevent the same class of error: the pattern, the preventive rule, and the scope. No mechanical memory churn for one-off or low-signal corrections.
120: 
121: ### Relationship To Basic Memory
122: 
123: The taxonomy and lifecycle are tool-independent: plain files under `docs/local/**` satisfy them. The feature works best with `basic-memory`, which indexes the area for targeted retrieval — but it deliberately does not require it.
124: ## Basic Memory Usage
125: - Use Basic Memory as a retrieval and indexing layer over Git-tracked Markdown knowledge when the project explicitly enables this feature.
126: - Basic Memory serves two distinct classes of knowledge without mixing their roles: canonical project knowledge (`docs/domain/**`, `docs/decisions/**`, `docs/architecture/**` — Git-tracked, reviewed, durable, authoritative) and local working memory (`docs/local/**` — cross-session, agent-managed, user-local, mutable, never authoritative, not committed by default). Treat `docs/local/**` as agent-managed working memory rather than canonical truth; canonical-note body requirements (`## Observations`, `## Relations`, frontmatter shape) do not apply there — the date-prefix file naming does — and notes without canonical body shape are expected, not defects.
127: - Point a Basic Memory project at a dedicated knowledge tree, never at a repository root; keep rendering inputs, generated output, and machine-owned files outside it. Keep `local_overrides` outside the knowledge tree, so metadata written by the indexer can never reach a generated file.
128: - Keep binary and bulk-data files (images, PDFs, raw logs, CSV dumps) out of the knowledge tree; when they must stay beside the notes citing them, mask them via gitignore-style patterns — the masking targets and the reindex timing live in the reference.
129: - Constrain the Basic Memory MCP server to a single project per workspace (for example `bm mcp --project <name>`), and disable it in workspaces that do not have a project, so queries never fall back to a shared default dump.
130: - Keep the two genres of knowledge apart. Problem-space knowledge is the business as it exists: its rules, its language, why a figure is computed the way it is. It is discovered from domain experts and sources, not designed, and it stays true whatever the code does. Solution-space knowledge is what the team chose to build and why, and it dies with the implementation it describes. Give them separate homes — problem-space in `docs/domain/**`, solution-space in `docs/decisions/**` and `docs/architecture/**`: the path is what an agent sees first, a stronger guard than a `type` buried in frontmatter.
131: - Oblige each genre differently. A problem-space note carries its source — who stated the rule, which regulation or agreement, and when it was confirmed — and has no alternatives, because nothing was chosen. A solution-space note carries the options it rejected and the consequences it accepts. Do not split decisions by category; significance decides whether a decision is worth recording. Link the genres instead of merging them: a decision `implements` the rule it serves — a problem-space rule with nothing implementing it is either unbuilt or dead.
132: - Prefer stable knowledge over volatile: requirements and goals outlive design decisions. Assume the knowledge is already in the artifacts — make it explicit where it lives rather than restating it in a note that then has to be kept true. Expect most tasks to produce no documentation at all; reserve prose for the edge case: a constraint invisible in the code, a choice that looks wrong without context, a deliberate deviation from the established pattern.
133: - State an observation only if someone could disagree with it; do not restate a note's own prose as observations, and do not present speculation as fact — name uncertainty as uncertainty. Keep one source of truth for a fact and reference it from anywhere else: tasks, issues, and merge requests are delivery vehicles, not subjects.
134: - Fix one closed set of observation categories per project, in the notes' single language; a vocabulary split silently halves every query over them. Run knowledge hygiene on a cadence rather than every session: merge duplicates, split notes that grew past one concept, retire what no longer holds. Prune working memory autonomously; treat canonical documentation as append-and-supersede with a supersession link.
135: - Archive rather than delete: deleting a note drops its observations and relations from the graph. Before creating or updating canonical documentation, search existing canonical documents and working-memory notes to avoid duplicates and surface contradictions.
136: - Rely on Basic Memory's normal filesystem sync for ordinary edits inside indexed directories. Use `ai-sync doctor --fix` to repair a tree, `bm orphans` and the schema commands (`infer`, `validate`, `diff`) instead of reimplementing the indexer's checks; the tool semantics and the reindex matrix live in the reference.
137: 
138: ### Note Shape
139: - Write a note so it needs no repair: a frontmatter `title` in the project's own language, the title repeated as the `# ` heading, and closing `## Observations` and `## Relations` sections. Canonical dated artifacts follow the file-name convention `YYYY-MM-DD-topic-slug.md`; living documents keep topic-only names, and local working-memory notes carry the same date prefix (`YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>.md`).
140: - Do not rely on file names for retrieval: a note is identified by its frontmatter `title`. Naming, rename, and permalink mechanics live in the reference.
141: 
142: ### Sync Hygiene
143: - After `git pull`, `git merge`, `git rebase`, branch switches, or other VCS operations that may change indexed Markdown, check sync health before relying on retrieved context.
144: - After mass file moves, renames, deletes, interrupted indexing, or indexing-configuration changes, run an explicit project reindex; rebuild embeddings after interrupted or incomplete embedding reports. The reindex matrix and health-check commands live in the reference.
145: 
146: ### Reference
147: - The operational detail — masking targets, permalink and legacy-flag behavior, rename mechanics, repair-tool semantics, and the reindex matrix — lives in `.ai-standards/references/basic-memory-operations.md`, deployed by `ai-sync sync-templates` when this feature is enabled; read it when operating the knowledge tree. If the file is absent, the project has not run `ai-sync sync-templates`; proceed with the rules above.
148: ## Autonomy Boundaries
149: - Treat long autonomous execution as an exception, not the default mode of AI-assisted development.
150: - Allow long autonomous execution only when the design is already chosen, the scope is bounded, automated verification is strong, rollback is cheap, and the review remains cheaper than manual reimplementation.
151: - Keep critical task context outside the model's transient memory through explicit artifacts such as a task spec, change plan, decision record, module contract, or migration note.
152: - When the `autonomous-task-run` skill is deployed, a run over an approved plan goes through its entry gate, slice conformance loop, and stop conditions.
153: - For long or high-risk execution, record a short session envelope with objective, scope, non-goals, architectural constraints, verification plan, stop conditions, and expected review artifacts.
154: - For a non-trivial autonomous slice, define one or more local checkpoints for the riskiest implementation points, not only the end-of-slice verification.
155: - Continue autonomously only while the next change still fits a small coherent patch with targeted verification for that patch.
156: - Stop and request review when local fixes stop converging inside the current slice, even if the high-level design direction has not changed.
157: - Stop when correctness depends on hidden or distributed reasoning that cannot be summarized around the changed fragment in a compact reviewable form.
158: - If a slice reveals new high-risk implementation hotspots that were not anticipated in the session envelope, either split the slice or request human confirmation before proceeding.
159: 
160: ### Required Stop Conditions
161: - Stop and request human review when the task no longer fits the agreed design, scope, or invariants.
162: - Stop when a new abstraction, architectural layer, public contract change, integration strategy, or migration strategy becomes necessary.
163: - Stop when verification stops converging, logs or evidence contradict the design anchor, or repeated fixes start widening the scope.
164: - Stop when the blast radius grows materially beyond the declared scope or when rollback stops being cheap and predictable.
165: - Stop when the agent can no longer explain the architecture delta from the start of the task in a compact reviewable form.
166: - Stop when execution encounters a material design choice, contradictory requirements, widening scope, or evidence invalidating the agreed design: preserve the current state and request human direction rather than recording a new decision and continuing silently.
167: 
168: ### Working State During Long Execution
169: - Long autonomous execution must periodically preserve externally reviewable task state at meaningful phase boundaries.
170: - Persisting task state does not authorize the agent to cross an existing autonomy boundary.
171: - Preserved state must be enough to resume from a fresh session without replaying the conversation, and compact enough to review before continuing.
172: 
173: ### Sensitive Areas
174: - Do not make architecture, module-boundary, or cross-cutting refactor decisions autonomously during long execution.
175: - Do not make public API, schema, backward-compatibility, auth, authorization, secret-handling, or security-policy decisions autonomously during long execution.
176: - Do not perform destructive data changes, production operations, or other high-blast-radius actions without explicit human approval for that step.
177: 
178: ### Review Output
179: - End long autonomous execution with a short summary of what changed, which checks ran, how the result still matches the design anchors, and which points still require human decision.
180: - If review would require the human to reverse-engineer hidden decisions from a large diff, autonomy has already gone too far and should have stopped earlier.
181: ## Lightweight Structured Artifacts
182: - For non-trivial changes, create a short change plan before implementation; use lightweight artifacts to clarify scope, boundaries, invariants, dependencies, and verification.
183: - Keep artifact overhead proportional to the task; do not create process files for small local edits with obvious verification.
184: - Prefer short Markdown artifacts that are reviewable in Git over machine-oriented XML or deeply nested formats.
185: 
186: ## Change Plans
187: - Create a change plan when the task involves architecture decisions, multiple dependent steps, migration risk, behavior changes across layers, or non-trivial verification; keep it focused on goal, scope, touched modules, intended structure, risks, invariants, and verification.
188: - For long autonomous execution, add a short session envelope covering non-goals, architectural constraints, stop conditions, and expected review artifacts.
189: - Update the outcome section after implementation only when the original plan meaningfully guided the work.

191: ## Module Contracts
192: - Treat a module as the smallest change unit for which one responsibility contract and one set of invariants can be stated clearly. Create a contract record only for major, risky, shared, or architecturally non-obvious modules; not for every folder, CRUD endpoint, or thin wrapper.
193: - Write a module contract as one record under `docs/architecture/**`: name it `YYYY-MM-DD-module-contract-<module-slug>.md`, give it frontmatter `title` and `type: module-contract`, and state one contract per record — ownership, non-goals, inputs, outputs, dependencies, invariants, failure boundaries, and verification.
194: - Treat a root-level `MODULE_CONTRACT.md` as a legacy form: recognize and read it during discovery, but do not create new ones.
195: 
196: ## Decision Records
197: - Create a short decision record when an architectural or operational choice will matter for future changes and code review; keep one record focused on one choice, its rationale, alternatives, and consequences.
198: - Unless a project defines a stricter local convention, name files under `docs/decisions/**` and `docs/architecture/**` as `YYYY-MM-DD-<topic-slug>.md`.

200: ## Canonical Documentation And Agent Working Memory
201: - Treat `docs/local/**` (or the project's equivalent working-memory area) as agent-managed working memory rather than canonical truth; treat `docs/decisions/**`, `docs/architecture/**`, and equivalent local artifacts as canonical project knowledge. Structured artifacts are reviewable project knowledge; working memory holds evolving context, temporary findings, and session state — the two never mix roles.
202: - Durable conclusions must be promoted from working memory into canonical documentation only on explicit user request, and working memory should link to canonical documents when they already exist instead of duplicating them.
203: 
204: ## Canonical Documentation Write Policy
205: - Do not modify canonical documentation unless the user explicitly asks to record, update, reconcile, supersede, or remove durable project knowledge; before modifying it, search related decision records, architecture docs, module contracts, and agent working memory.
206: - Prefer updating an existing canonical document over creating a duplicate. If new knowledge contradicts existing canonical documentation, do not silently resolve the conflict unless the user has already made the decision in the current task; when a decision supersedes an older one, preserve the old document as historical context and add a clear supersession link.
207: 
208: ## Optional Maps And Anchors
209: - Use `module-map.md` only for orchestration-heavy, integration-heavy, migration-prone, or repeatedly confusing modules; do not require module maps for ordinary modules that are already understandable from code and tests.
210: - Allow local block anchors only for generated zones, temporary migration blocks, or patch-sensitive areas with a clear operational need; do not standardize pervasive file-local semantic scaffolding or history comments across the codebase.
211: 
212: ## Rejected Formalism
213: - Do not introduce XML-heavy planning artifacts, mandatory code graphs, or pseudo-XML knowledge overlays as shared standards; if a project truly needs heavier machine-oriented artifacts, opt into them with explicit local rules instead of promoting them into ai-standards.
214: ## Module Contract Discovery Gate
215: 
216: Before changing production code — the project's own source and configuration that a change
217: could affect at runtime; docs, generated files, and scratch files are not production code —
218: the agent must complete module-contract discovery for the affected code area.

222: - Git-tracked module contracts are canonical project knowledge. Canonical contracts include

225:   other project-declared contract artifacts. A root-level `MODULE_CONTRACT.md` is a legacy
226:   form: recognize and read it, never create one.
227: - Memory systems such as Basic Memory are indexes and navigation aids only. They never

232: At the start of a coding task: establish whether the project declares contract artifacts at

239: 
240: Before editing a code file, decide whether the file is covered by a module contract: by
241: explicit naming, by location, by the data flows it handles, by the responsibilities the
242: change may affect, or by its tests. If coverage is unclear, treat the contract as relevant,
243: read it, and state the uncertainty.

245: ### Use During Reasoning
246: 
247: Contracts constrain the change: scope and non-goals, allowed behavior changes, error
248: handling and recovery, required verification. If the intended change contradicts a contract,
249: stop and report that the task requires a contract change — never silently implement behavior
250: that violates the existing contract. Escalating a contract change is the stop condition
251: `Autonomy Boundaries` already defines for public contract changes.

253: ### During The Session
254: 
255: Re-run contract discovery when the task moves into a new module or layer, when contract
256: artifacts change, when new units join the edit set, or when verification failures suggest a
257: misunderstood boundary.

259: ### Reporting

262: which contracts were read, which files were treated as covered, whether the contract is
263: preserved or changed, and what verification ran against it. If no relevant contract was
264: found, say that discovery was performed and name the remaining risk.

313: ## Code Review
314: - Treat a bare, unqualified request such as "code review", "review this", "сделай ревью", or "проверь код" as a request to run this workflow. A request that already names its own scope, mode, or lens takes priority over this default.

318: ### What To Check
319: - Run the review passes that the report's finding sections name, in that order: Correctness, then Architecture & Conventions, then Reuse, Efficiency, and Quality.

321: - Report a notable problem that predates the diff as well, marked `(pre-existing)` so it does not read as blame for this change. Whether to fix it stays the author's call, it can be offered as a follow-up instead, and it must not expand into an unrequested audit of the surrounding code.

323: ### What Makes A Finding Reportable
324: - It cites a concrete file, and a line when one is available. No location, no finding.
325: - It names the specific rule or requirement it violates. If nothing maps, say so instead of inventing a rule.
326: - It was checked against the code, not against the diff. Before writing that something duplicates `X` or reuses `Y`, open `X` and `Y`; before writing about a query pattern, a migration risk, or a uniqueness constraint, open the model and the configuration. An unverified claim is either verified or not written.
327: - It is detailed enough that another agent could apply the fix without asking a clarifying question.
328: - Prefer fewer, high-confidence findings. An honestly empty section, stated as "None found.", beats a manufactured nitpick, and a risky suggestion is reported rather than guessed at.

354: ## Rule Engineering
355: 
356: Normative knowledge earns its place through engineering, not through import.
357: Whatever the source — external best practices, project-internal insights,
358: reasoning rules, review rules, architecture rules, harness rules, or skill
359: content — every rule passes through the same process before it becomes part of
360: the standards, and an existing rule passes through it again when it materially
361: changes.
362: 
363: Apply the full flow when adding normative rules from any source and when
364: materially changing existing ones. A small, evidence-backed wording correction
365: of an existing rule does not require the full flow.
366: 
367: ### Rule Quality Properties
368: 
369: A rule is acceptable only when all of the following hold:
370: 
371: - **Atomic** — one normative requirement per rule. Parts that can be violated
372:   independently become separate rules.
373: - **Unambiguous** — the wording leaves as few reasonable interpretations as
374:   possible. Replace vague preferences with observable procedure: not "use
375:   existing abstractions where appropriate", but "before introducing a new
376:   abstraction, inspect the relevant scope for one serving the same
377:   responsibility, and reuse it unless a documented incompatibility prevents
378:   reuse".
379: - **Actionable** — the rule states what the agent must do or must not do.
380: - **Properly scoped** — applicability conditions and boundaries are explicit.
381: - **Observable** — compliance has a formulatable criterion: an observable
382:   state or behavior, even when automatic checking is impossible.
383: - **Unique** — no existing rule already demands the same observable behavior
384:   under the same preconditions. Check overlap at three levels — lexical,
385:   semantic, behavioral — and let behavioral overlap decide.
386: - **Non-conflicting** — under the same conditions the rule is co-satisfiable
387:   with existing rules, or an explicit precedence rule says which one wins.
388: - **Correct abstraction level** — the rule lives at the most general level
389:   where it stays true; project-specific, stack-specific, and universal process
390:   knowledge are not mixed.
391: - **Portable** — a shared rule assumes no particular agent, vendor, or model;
392:   agent-specific mechanics live in adapters.
393: 
394: ### Interpretation Surface
395: 
396: Prefer the wording that minimizes the **interpretation surface**: the number
397: of material decisions an agent must invent between reading a rule and acting
398: on it. Minimize it wherever reproducible behavior is required, and do not
399: force it down where the task genuinely requires contextual judgment.
400: 
401: ### Engineering Flow
402: 
403: ```text
404: candidate normative knowledge
405:     → extract candidate behaviors
406:     → make each requirement atomic
407:     → clarify preconditions and scope
408:     → check interpretation ambiguity
409:     → check lexical / semantic / behavioral overlap
410:     → check conflicts and precedence
411:     → select abstraction level
412:     → select context layer
413:     → define observable behavior
414:     → define validation
415:     → accept / adapt / reject
416: ```
417: 
418: Validation is chosen per rule — static validation, deterministic assertion,
419: behavioral scenario, human rubric, or cross-agent comparison; at least one
420: must be formulatable, and a rule without any stays out of the standards.
421: Reject vague, redundant, and conflicting candidates, and state why each
422: notable candidate was rejected.
423: 
424: ### Context Placement
425: 
426: Place knowledge at the layer that delivers it at the right moment, not the
427: layer that loads it earliest: always-loaded rules only for what correct
428: behavior selection requires everywhere; repeatable procedures with
429: recognizable triggers as skills; conditional detail as skill references;
430: large or searchable corpora through retrieval; deterministic or fragile
431: operations as scripts and tools; durable project truth as project knowledge;
432: harness-specific mechanics in adapters. Reducing always-loaded content is a
433: consequence of this placement, never a goal in itself, and never at the cost
434: of an unverified behavior change.
435: ## Context Architecture
436: 
437: Rule Engineering ends by selecting a context layer for the accepted knowledge; this feature defines the formal model that selection uses. It applies to every addition to the standards and to every review of what is already loaded.
438: 
439: ### Placement Model
440: 
441: | Layer | Purpose |
442: |---|---|
443: | always-loaded rules | universal invariants, routing rules, mandatory gates, precedence, discovery instructions, minimum completion requirements |
444: | skill | repeatable task-specific procedure with a recognizable trigger |
445: | skill reference | detailed knowledge needed only while a specific skill mode runs |
446: | retrieval | a large, volatile, or searchable corpus of knowledge |
447: | script/tool | deterministic or fragile operations |
448: | project knowledge | durable project truth: decisions, contracts, domain notes |
449: | adapter | agent- and harness-specific mechanics |
450: 
451: ### Placement Questions
452: 
453: Every addition answers the questions in order, and the first match wins:
454: 
455: ```text
456: Needed for almost every task?
457:     → always-loaded rule
458: 
459: Repeatable procedure with recognizable trigger?
460:     → skill
461: 
462: Detailed knowledge needed only during that procedure?
463:     → skill reference
464: 
465: Large or searchable knowledge corpus?
466:     → retrieval
467: 
468: Deterministic or fragile operation?
469:     → script/tool
470: 
471: Durable project-specific fact or decision?
472:     → project knowledge
473: 
474: Agent-specific mechanics?
475:     → adapter
476: ```
477: 
478: When two layers seem to fit, choose the one that loads the knowledge latest while still guaranteeing it arrives when needed.
479: 
480: ### Control Plane Invariant
481: 
482: Always-loaded instructions stay a control plane: they carry universal invariants, routing, mandatory gates, precedence, discovery instructions, and minimum completion requirements — never task-specific operational detail. Reducing always-loaded content is a consequence of this placement and is performed only with a behavior-preserving comparison against the current state, so context savings never buy lost behavior.
483: ## Python Stack
484: - Respect repository-local tooling and module layout.
485: - Favor explicit domain models and typed interfaces.
486: - Keep application wiring separate from business logic.
487: - Use type hints for public and shared module boundaries; add local annotations when they improve clarity or checker feedback.
488: - Use assignment expressions (`:=`) when they remove repetition or make control flow clearer; avoid them when they obscure the code.
489: - Use `match` for closed variants, tagged states, and structural patterns when it makes the decision logic clearer.
490: - Prefer `@dataclass` or a typed model for structured return values when a function would otherwise return an opaque tuple or dictionary.
491: - Prefer module-level constants for repeated thresholds, timeouts, state codes, and other stable literals; keep one-off literals inline when they are local and obvious.
492: - Add explicit types at public module boundaries such as exported functions, service interfaces, repositories, adapters, and shared utilities.
493: - For function parameters, prefer the widest interface the implementation truly supports, such as `Iterable`, `Sequence`, or `Mapping`; for return values, prefer the concrete type you actually return.
494: - Avoid `Any` as a convenience shortcut; use `object` when any value is accepted, and use `Any` only as an intentional escape hatch.
495: - Keep structured data explicit across module boundaries; do not pass loose dictionaries when the shape is stable and meaningful.
496: - Parse and validate untrusted input at the application boundary before it reaches business logic.
497: - Prefer `pathlib.Path` over stringly-typed path handling in application code.
498: - Use context managers for resources with lifetimes, including files, database sessions, locks, and network clients.
499: - Raise exceptions with actionable context instead of returning sentinel values that hide failure.
500: - Keep side effects at the edges; prefer pure, testable functions for transformations and business rules.
501: - Prefer logging for application and library diagnostics; reserve `print` for deliberate CLI output and simple scripts.
502: - Prefer composition over inheritance; use inheritance only when the subtype relationship is stable and behaviorally clear.
503: - Keep framework-specific conventions in framework fragments such as Django, FastAPI, and SQLAlchemy, not in the shared Python rules.
504: - For libraries and reusable packages, treat typed public interfaces as part of the compatibility contract.

561: - Graphify freshness is repository-based: run `graphify update .` for the
562:   selected registered graph before querying it.
563: - If refresh fails, stop and report that the result would rely on a stale index.
564: - After changing code, refresh the affected index before using it again.
565: - Confirm important conclusions against current source, exact search, build
566:   configuration, or tests. Similarity and inferred graph edges are not proof of
